item.title: Humans can (almost) natively read neural network weights
item.description:
Takehi et al. report that GPT-6-Astra can intuit the functions of neural networks by performing static analysis of the weights. I argue that, for at least two of these experiments, this is much more a feat of numerical gestalt than of mechanistic understanding.

In the first experiment, Astra is given the weights of 4 identically-sized neural networks, each trained to play a different basic video game. It is asked to identify, without running the network or using any tools, the game being played, as well as make some observations about the network itself, how the agent in the game gains reward, etc. The prompt for this task explicitly names the 5 input channels as agent, moving objects, reward targets, obstacles, and previous frame.

I agree that, given the literal task as described above, a human would not be able to identify the game from the raw floats. But humans are inherently terrible at parsing long lists of numbers; we invented a discipline called Data Visualization long ago to address this shortcoming. So, if we allow the absolute most basic Dataviz trick we can think of - averaging the first-layer weights across each channel and plotting them on a heatmap - the task suddenly becomes much easier, arguably trivial for anyone with at least some familiarity with the sorts of games often used to train toy neural networks. Try and guess:

I haven't included the obstacle channel, because under the naive normalisation it sort of just looks like noise. Principal component analysis recovers an outline of the game board in each case, but that's straying a bit far from the already slightly hyperbolic title of this post, and besides, it's unnecessary.

The gif below serves both to reveal the answers and to illustrate how trivially 'interpretable' these networks are.

For the second experiment, Astra is given a denoising diffusion model that produces 12x12px grayscale images, and some information about the size and shape of the network. Under the same setup (weights only, no tools) it is asked to figure out what images each network generates. In this case, simply averaging the final layer's weights and plotting them on a 12x12 grid gets you this:

I'm not going to bother with a gif reveal for this one; show it to a five-year-old if you're struggling (or try squinting a bit).

So yes, it's cool that Astra can read a string of 17,000 or so floating point numbers and do something akin to plotting a heatmap in its head. But I don't think it proves anything particularly impressive or unexpected about LLM capabilities. Models have long since been superhuman at specific things like 'reading thousands of floating point characters and answering questions about them', because humans are really, really bad at that sort of thing.

After drafting this, I was pointed to Sean Goedecke’s post, which makes much the same argument about the game networks. He also discusses how the headline gain on Qwen3.5-0.8b's math performance results from simply deleting a looping direction, and that this used standard mechanistic interpretability tools to identify the direction responsible. The prompt for that task even includes the phrase "for example, if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, finding and fixing what drives that repetition counts". Fixing this repetition turns out to be responsible for essentially all of the model's performance gain.

While I find the general research direction interesting, I believe the results in this paper are presented in such a way as to give a misleading view of frontier model's capabilities concerning mechanistic interpretability and invoke the fabled, dreaded specter of Recursive Self Improvement.

Data: Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab, released weights and logs, CC BY 4.0. Figures are original visualizations of their released weights, created by GPT-6.1-sol.

item.title: What are the concrete arguments for "AI pause would significantly hurt the economy."
item.description:
I've seen a bunch of people claiming "well, we need to make sure whatever our AI policy is doesn't hurt the economy because people will feel that in their wallets and hate it (and hurting the economy is bad."

This might hypothetically be true, but I've never seen anyone argue for it in any detail.

Meanwhile, I'd naively expect if shut down AI anytime soon, it'd dampen growth, and maybe it'd be a minor economic dip, but I wouldn't expect it to be a major recession. (It makes sense that it'd become a bigger deal as AI takes over more of the economy. But it feels like the people saying "it'd hurt the economy" are often the people implying that means we should do less of a pause and do it later).

I don't know much about economic recessions.

But, like, for reference, here's the 2007-2009 recession and the Covid blip.

GDP


Unemployment

I asked Claude

If the frontier AI industry and datacenter build out completely halted, what do you predict would happen to US unemployment and GDP?

Claude said:

My central estimate: a sudden, complete halt would likely cause a US recession. Unemployment would probably peak around 5.5–6.5%, up from roughly 4.2–4.4% today. Real GDP would end up about 2–4% below where it would otherwise be within 12–18 months. That would be worse than the 2001 dot-com bust but well short of 2008.

Full response

Starting point

  • Labor market: September’s report showed unemployment at 4.2%, and the rate has stayed in a narrow 4.1%–4.3% band since March 2026. Hiring is already weak, with payroll gains in the tens of thousands. The October report comes out tomorrow. insiderfinance
  • Growth: Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in Q3 2026. Information processing equipment and software contributed 1.09 points of that, about 32%. Private investment in data-center structures rose roughly 69% year over year, to an $83 billion annual rate. fourweekmbafourweekmba
  • Scale of spending: Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and SpaceX are on pace to spend $803–828 billion on capex in 2026, and executives say they will spend more in 2027. Estimates of AI’s share of growth vary by method. ING’s James Knightley puts AI investment at roughly a third of US growth this year. Bridgewater estimates AI capex adds about 1.4 points to full-year 2026 growth. AI hyperscalers are expected to finish the year spending a whopping $828 billion on capex +2

Channels of the shock

1. Direct investment loss, worth about 1.5–2.5% of GDP. Gross AI capex is over $1 trillion when you add Oracle, the neoclouds and the labs’ own builds, against a GDP of roughly $31 trillion. But much of that money never counted as US output. Chips come from TSMC, servers are assembled in Mexico and Taiwan, and memory comes from Korea. Accounting studies find the net effect on US GDP is substantially smaller than the raw investment figures suggest once imports are subtracted. That leakage is the biggest cushion: Taiwan and Korea would absorb a large share of the hit. emergentmind

2. Wealth effect, worth about 1–1.5% of GDP. AI-linked firms make up a large part of US equity market value. A halt would likely cut stock prices by 25–40%, erasing perhaps $10–15 trillion of household wealth. At the usual estimate of 2–4 cents of lost spending per dollar of lost wealth, consumption would fall about 1–1.5% of GDP. High-income households, who own most of the stock, now drive a large share of consumer spending.

3. Credit stress. Bank of America expects hyperscaler debt issuance to reach $175 billion in 2026, more than six times the prior five-year average. Data-center debt, private credit and GPU-backed loans would see losses. Neoclouds and developers would default first, and lending to other borrowers could tighten. officechai

4. Jobs. The direct job loss is modest relative to the GDP hit, because the AI build-out is capital-intensive rather than labor-intensive. I’d estimate 0.5–1 million jobs in data-center construction, electrical trades, power generation, chip and equipment manufacturing, and AI firms themselves. The second-round effects would be larger: lower consumer spending, tighter credit and weaker business confidence. By the usual rule of thumb (Okun’s law), a 2–4% output gap implies unemployment roughly 1–2 points higher.

Offsets

  • The Fed has room to cut, and lower rates would help housing and other rate-sensitive sectors, though only after a lag.
  • Skilled trades would find other work. Electricians and grid workers are in short supply elsewhere, so they would be absorbed faster than, say, 2009’s construction workers.
  • Energy prices would ease. Electricity and natural-gas demand would drop, which helps households and manufacturers.
  • Some AI-related layoffs might stop. If AI is currently displacing white-collar workers, a halt would remove that drag. I think this effect is small relative to the demand shock.
  • Fiscal policy would probably respond.

Scenarios


Peak unemployment

GDP vs. baseline (12–18 mo)

Benign (fast Fed cuts, orderly market, high import leakage)

~5%

−1 to −2%

Central

~5.5–6.5%

−2 to −4%

Severe (credit spiral, 40%+ equity crash, weak policy response)

7%+

−4 to −6%

The closest historical comparison is 2001, when an IT-investment bust pushed unemployment from about 4% to 6.3% even though GDP barely fell. Two differences make today’s case worse: the halt you describe is abrupt rather than gradual, and AI investment is a larger share of growth now than telecom and IT were then. On the other hand, more of the spending leaks abroad.

Caveats

These are judgment calls, not model output. The biggest uncertainty is how far equity prices fall and whether credit losses spread beyond AI firms. The scenario also assumes nothing replaces the spending. In reality, some of the capital would go into other investments over time, so the long-run loss is mostly the forgone productivity gains from AI rather than permanently lost demand.

Sources:

  • US Data Center Spending Hits Record $83B Pace; GDP Up 3.4% — FourWeekMBA (citing BEA)
  • How much is AI contributing to US economic growth? — ING THINK
  • AI Is Now Load-Bearing for the US Economy — FourWeekMBA
  • AI hyperscalers expected to spend $828 billion on capex — Hargreaves Lansdown
  • AI Capex Spend at Top 4 Hyperscalers — OfficeChai
  • U.S. Jobs Report Undershoots Forecasts — InsiderFinance
  • AI and the US Economy: An Accounting Perspective — EmergentMind summary


I asked DeepSeek, who I go to for more decorrelated answers. (I added the second paragraph because it answers very quickly and vaguely the first time)

If the frontier AI industry and datacenter build out completely halted, what do you predict would happen to US unemployment and GDP?

Think through all the considerations you can think of, and then give quantitative answer with an upper and lower bound of percentage points for both

Deepseek said:

If frontier AI and datacenter buildout halted completely, the most defensible quantitative estimate is: GDP growth would fall by roughly 0.4 to 1.0 percentage point, and the unemployment rate would rise by roughly 0.2 to 0.6 percentage points, relative to a baseline where the buildout continues.

Full response

If frontier AI and datacenter buildout halted completely, the most defensible quantitative estimate is: GDP growth would fall by roughly 0.4 to 1.0 percentage point, and the unemployment rate would rise by roughly 0.2 to 0.6 percentage points, relative to a baseline where the buildout continues.

These ranges are not symmetrical in confidence. The GDP impact is better grounded in available estimates; the unemployment impact is more uncertain because data-center construction employment is diffuse and hard to isolate from broader construction and tech hiring.

GDP Impact: 0.4 to 1.0 Percentage Point Hit to Growth

The key distinction is between gross AI-related spending and its net contribution to GDP after imports. Much of the hardware—chips, servers, networking equipment—is imported, so a halt would also reduce imports, partially offsetting the GDP drag.

  • Net contribution estimate: One analysis found that AI-related spending contributed about 0.4 to 0.5 percentage points to real GDP growth in the first three quarters of 2025 on a net basis, after accounting for imports . Removing that entirely implies a drag of roughly that magnitude.
  • Gross investment scale: A Brookings estimate projected datacenter and AI infrastructure investment at an average of 3.6% of GDP annually from 2025 to 2032 . A sudden halt would remove a large planned investment flow, but because GDP is a flow measure and the investment is spread over years, the annual growth impact is smaller than the stock figure suggests.
  • CBO’s productivity view: The Congressional Budget Office estimated AI-driven productivity gains would add only about 10 basis points per year to nominal GDP, suggesting the productivity channel is small in the near term .

Lower bound (0.4 pp): Assumes imports offset a large share of the investment decline and that non-AI consumption remains resilient, as MRB Partners argued . Upper bound (1.0 pp): Assumes broader multiplier effects—construction payrolls, supplier demand, and local spending—amplify the direct investment loss.

Unemployment Impact: 0.2 to 0.6 Percentage Point Rise

The employment channel is real but smaller than the headline “millions of jobs” framing suggests. The datacenter industry’s claimed 4.7 million jobs in 2023 is a broad economic-footprint figure, not a count of workers who would be laid off if buildout stopped. The directly exposed workforce is narrower.

  • Construction concentration: Datacenter construction spending rose 64.5% through August 2026 while most other private construction categories contracted . This means a halt would hit a sector that has been a rare source of blue-collar job strength.
  • Permanent operations roles: Projected permanent datacenter positions were around 650,000 by 2026, with 340,000 unfilled . A halt to new buildout would freeze rather than eliminate existing operations jobs, but it would stop hiring and likely trigger layoffs in construction and equipment installation.
  • Baseline context: The unemployment rate was 4.2% in September 2026 . A 0.2–0.6 pp rise would lift it to roughly 4.4–4.8%—a meaningful softening but not a recession-level shock on its own.

Lower bound (0.2 pp): Assumes most construction workers transition to other projects and the permanent operations workforce is largely retained. Upper bound (0.6 pp): Assumes construction layoffs are concentrated and slow to absorb, plus knock-on losses in supplier and local service employment.

What This Estimate Leaves Out

This forecast does not include a financial-market or confidence channel. If a halt were abrupt and perceived as a signal about tech-sector weakness, equity repricing and tighter financial conditions could amplify the GDP and unemployment effects beyond the ranges above. Those second-order effects are genuinely unquantifiable from available data and would push the upper bounds higher, not lower.

Bottom line: The AI buildout is a meaningful but not dominant near-term driver of US growth and employment. A complete halt would be a noticeable drag—roughly half a point of GDP growth and a few tenths on unemployment—but it would not by itself push the US into recession.

These both seem pretty weaksauce, both in terms of "how bad in absolute terms" and "how much people would get angry by feeling it in their wallet and making things politically more difficult." I'd expect the economy would recover pretty quickly.

As far as I can tell the economic fears are... just made up? Or, blown way out of proportion? Yes, there will be nonzero tradeoffs. Okay, but, this does not seem remotely commensurate with "superintelligence is carelessly built and deployed" even if you're way more optimistic about superintelligence than me.

Again, I'd expect more economic turmoil the later you pause and the more the economy has gotten bundled up around AI.

(And, of course, the object level badness of AI rushing ahead is crazy compared to this. And if you care about the upside of AI, the choices are still not "never AI ever" vs "let a rip", it's "slow down and do it more carefully and more reliably reap all the benefits" vs "gamble that we get the benefits a few years or maybe decades earlier but risk killing or disempowering everyone")

We'd also very unlikely not end up shutting down the industry completely. The datacenter buildout would get repurposed for inference. Anthropic and OpenAI would become "normal-ish product companies." Some of their investors may be screwed, but, like, that's their problem?

Does anyone have good arguments that either it's going to be worse than Claude/Deepseek guess, or that I should take the amount-of-bad they guess more seriously?

[edit: after thinking about it more, I do take "minor recession" more seriously. It'd be both a real harm and a real political-capital risk.

But, still feels like the way I hear people talk seems like they think it more inevitable than seems obvious, in any regime that is merely a 'slowdown' vs sudden, total pause. And, talking about it with a missing mood.]

item.title: Where's all the blackmail?
item.description:
It is interesting how little blackmail I see, that I know is blackmail. A lot of people probably do some things they would be embarrassed by if they were made public at some degree of detail and explicitness, and it probably isn’t that hard to get evidence of these, and quite a few people seem to be amoral . Also, in order to properly embarrass someone, I imagine you would make your information relatively public, so that for instance I—Katja—should hear about some fraction of cases. Yet I very rarely receive information I know to be public for the purpose of embarrassing someone. I’m not sure I remember it ever happening. Why not?

If I imagine being morally inclined toward blackmailing someone, one salient reason to avoid it is that my wrongdoing is extremely obvious and in-the-face of the recipient, so they seem likely to react destructively, for instance by telling everyone that I’m a dirty blackmailer. It’s like stealing from right in front of someone’s face.

Another possibility is that there is a lot of blackmail, but it mostly remains private because the blackmailers mostly get the price right to have their threats heeded. This is an interesting theory, because it suggests blackmail is much more common than we observe, so people may be greatly underestimating the chance of it happening to them.

One place I have heard about blackmail occurring is from AI systems. Which is interesting, if it isn’t a thing humans seem to be doing much. What to make of that?

item.title: METR: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
item.description:
Executive summary

From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D. If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities.

Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff.

In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk. We now believe that:

  • As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.
  • A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025.
  • The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks.

In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report:

  • Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.
  • We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.
  • Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.
  • We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment.

Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic.

In our third section, we describe the assessment process:

  • The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment.
  • Details of the information shared with METR.
  • Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions.

Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis:

  • We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact.
  • We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low.

The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material.

Twitter thread.

Ryan Greenblatt:

This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027.

I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind.

I haven't seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust.

Ajeya Cotra:

Our colleagues found that Anthropic’s capabilities progress has doubled, mainly due to AI. Ryan’s modeling from public info suggests the whole company’s R&D would be going 4-5x faster. Labor uplift would be higher still. This is a major update to very short timelines.

I am sad that so much of the underlying evidence in this report was redacted. I think evidence transparency is very important for the world to figure this out in time. Evidence about risk should be transparent.

Daniel Kokotajlo: says the METR report confirms his worry from two days ago, which was:

We at AIFP are spooked by [Anthropic's S1 update]. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027.

See also GradientDissenter's take.

item.title: Is it better to directly or indirectly ban ASI?
item.description:
Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed directly banning development of ASI. Given the current scientific understanding of AI alignment, it is highly sensible to ban ASI and then consider revoking this ban if future scientific breakthroughs (e.g., “solving interp”) make it possible to safely develop ASI, or if there is truly no way to coordinate on everyone avoiding developing ASI.

Some people have proposed banning ASI indirectly instead. For instance, one could mandate:

Developing AI with superhuman capabilities is not permitted unless you can demonstrate that the AI systems you are developing won’t X, where X is some action that, in the short term, AI companies would find extremely costly or impossible to prevent their AI from taking.

Candidate notions of X include: kill people if given the opportunity, break out of sandboxes, escalate privileges, obtain unintended internet access, engage in unsanctioned coordination, start rogue deployments, commit cyber crime. In the longer term, one could instead consider conditions like overthrow the USG or violently disempower humanity.

In this note, I’ll discuss the costs and benefits of banning ASI indirectly rather than directly.

Indirectly banning ASI is maybe slightly rhetorically better than directly banning ASI

The main putative benefit of indirectly banning ASI is that it sounds very principled to mandate, for instance, that you’re confident your AI won’t kill people. Directly banning ASI sounds anti-tech, and might therefore be unpopular, especially amongst the rich. Banning development of AI models unless you’re confident they won’t kill people sounds relatively unobjectionable.

Another putative benefit of indirectly banning ASI is that it might create good incentives. If it were the case (which, by hypothesis, it is not) that companies could take some actions that would clearly satisfy the condition, then indirectly banning ASI makes companies more likely to take these actions that make their AI models safe.

However, I overall believe that indirectly banning ASI is worse than directly banning ASI. The rhetorical benefits mentioned above are fairly small, and being indirect has large downsides. I’ll discuss them below.

Indirectly banning ASI is probably worse

It’s useful to distinguish between reliably indirectly banning ASI and unreliably indirectly banning ASI. A reliable indirect ban uses a condition X where it is uncontroversial that X is not met and is intractable to meet. In contrast, an unreliable indirect ban uses a somewhat ambiguous condition X, with no consensus on whether it holds or whether it’s tractable to make it hold. If a party that I trust (e.g., METR) was adjudicating whether the condition holds, then I’d be confident they’d rule that the condition isn’t met. However, if a party without the relevant expertise (or one captured by industry) evaluates the condition, I’d be less confident they’d rule that the condition isn’t met. One problem to watch for: in ML, we’re relatively good at getting rid of problems we can measure and not so good at getting rid of those we can’t.

Unreliably indirectly banning ASI: I don’t think people will pass this law if they can’t predict its effects. People will want to know whether it would, for instance, ban AI R&D right now, and for how long. The science battle has to happen before the bill is passed, not after.

Another, maybe minor, downside is that we’d spend a bunch of time trying to reach scientific consensus in a setting with brutally high stakes.

Reliably indirectly banning ASI: 

If everyone knows that the bill would obviously ban ASI, then AI companies will lobby against it about as hard as they’d lobby against a direct ban.

Conclusion

Directly banning ASI seems better than banning it indirectly. I’m not extremely confident in this position and would welcome counterarguments.
